title: 9/11 remains a vivid lived memory while national trauma shifts toward school, family, and generational transmission
source_unit: Pew Research Center, 9/11 memories remain vivid in the U.S. 25 years later, September 2026
geography: United States; adults nationally with age and generational comparisons

observations.period: August 24-30, 2026; memory among adults old enough to remember 9/11

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in Pew American Trends Panel survey

pre_2001_exact_memory.unit: percent of adults born before 2001 saying they remember exactly where they were or what they were doing when they heard the news

age_10_or_older_exact_memory.unit: percent of adults who were age 10 or older at the time reporting exact memory

age_30_exact_memory.unit: rolling five-year average estimate for age 30

age_40_exact_memory.unit: rolling five-year average estimate for age 40

age_50_exact_memory.unit: rolling five-year average estimate for age 50

observations.method: Pew Research Center survey of 5,166 U.S. adults in the American Trends Panel, fielded August 24-30, 2026; age-specific estimates use rolling five-year averages.
observations.uncertainty: Reported vivid memory is a self-assessment and does not measure accuracy, trauma, political interpretation, or later behavior; age patterns combine life-cycle, cohort, and event-exposure differences.
observations.subgroup: Adults born before 2001, adults age 10 or older on September 11, 2001, and younger adult age cohorts.
observations.counterinterpretation: High memory vividness does not imply shared meaning: people may remember the event clearly while disagreeing about causes, policy response, war, security, immigration, or national identity.

observations.period: 2026; adults born after the attacks and inherited knowledge

denominator.unit: U.S. adults in the Pew survey; younger-adult subgroup where specified

born_after_attacks.unit: percent of U.S. adults born after 2001 and therefore not direct witnesses

ages_18_24_learned_at_school.unit: percent of adults ages 18-24 saying they first learned about 9/11 in class or through schoolwork

ages_18_24_learned_family_friends.unit: percent of adults ages 18-24 saying they first learned through family or friends

ages_18_24_learned_independently.unit: percent saying they first learned by reading or watching something on their own

ages_18_24_unsure_learning_route.unit: percent unsure how they first learned about the attacks

observations.method: Pew survey questions about whether respondents were born after 2001 and how adults ages 18-24 first learned about the attacks.
observations.uncertainty: The first-learning route is self-reported and does not measure what was taught, remembered, emotionally experienced, or politically inferred; school exposure is not equivalent to curriculum quality or consensus.
observations.subgroup: Adults born after 2001, particularly those ages 18-24 in 2026.
observations.counterinterpretation: School-mediated knowledge can coexist with family stories, media exposure, community rituals, and personal research; transmission channels overlap even when respondents name one first source.

observations.period: 2001-2026; persistence and generational conversion of national trauma

denominator.unit: U.S. adult memory and historical-attitude frame across Pew surveys since the attacks

long_run_tracking.value: Pew has regularly measured reactions to 9/11 and related attitudes throughout the 25 years since the attacks

direct_memory_to_transmission_shift.value: As the directly affected population ages, a growing share of adults knows the attacks through school, family, friends, media, or other accounts

observations.method: Pew synthesis of the 2026 survey with prior post-attack and follow-up survey work.
observations.uncertainty: The source does not establish how memory transmission changes political attitudes, security preferences, intergroup relations, or national identity; historical survey comparability and cohort replacement remain analytical boundaries.
observations.subgroup: Direct witnesses, older adults, younger adults, and post-2001 birth cohorts.
observations.counterinterpretation: A national event can remain symbolically important while its political meaning changes across generations, institutions, media environments, and geopolitical contexts.

boundary: This record adds a cultural-memory and generational-transmission layer: 9/11 remains vividly remembered by those old enough to recall it, while younger Americans increasingly encounter it through school, family, friends, media, and inherited narratives. It does not establish memory accuracy, shared meaning, trauma prevalence, policy attitudes, national identity, or causal political effects.
